quests.instruction: Grandma wants a comfy spot to sit with her feet up and read for an hour. Which would you offer her?
quests.hint: Look for furniture made for one person to sit and relax in.
quests.explanation: An armchair has a seat, a back, and arms, so a person can sit comfortably for a long time. A side table holds things, and a rack holds clothes.
quests.funFact: Some armchairs lean back or have a footrest built in.

quests.instruction: Ben has to sit at a tall kitchen counter. Which seat is made for that height?
quests.hint: The seat has to lift him up to the counter's level.
quests.explanation: A tall stool raises the seat so a person can reach a high counter. A beanbag or cushion sits close to the floor.
quests.funFact: Stools have no back, so they tuck neatly under a counter when nobody is using them.

quests.instruction: Two sisters share a small bedroom and want more floor space. Which sleeping furniture would help?
quests.hint: Think about stacking instead of spreading out.
quests.explanation: A bunk bed puts one bed above another, so two people can sleep in the floor space of one.
quests.funFact: Safety guidelines say the top bunk is not for young children.

quests.instruction: Which piece of storage furniture has boxes that slide out?
quests.hint: Think of what you pull toward you when you look for your socks.
quests.explanation: Drawers slide in and out, so you can reach clothes and small things. Bookcases and shoe racks have open shelves instead.
quests.funFact: Small boxes or dividers inside a drawer keep little things from sliding into a jumble.

quests.instruction: A family wants to show off the covers of their books. What could they put the books on?
quests.hint: Choose furniture that lets you see what is inside without opening anything.
quests.explanation: Open shelves let you see the covers at a glance. A cupboard with doors hides what is inside, and a coat stand is made for coats.
quests.funFact: Libraries shelve books upright with the spines facing out, so titles are easy to scan.

quests.instruction: Why do many cupboards have doors?
quests.correctAnswer: To hide things and keep dust off 🚪
options: To hide things and keep dust off 🚪
quests.hint: Open shelves show everything. What do doors change?
quests.explanation: Doors hide clutter and keep dust, and sometimes little hands, away from what is inside. They do not change weight or temperature.
quests.funFact: Cupboards that hold cleaning supplies often have child locks.

quests.instruction: Hot soup is ready to serve. Which dish keeps it from running off?
quests.hint: Soup is a liquid, so the dish needs high sides.
quests.explanation: A bowl has deep, curved sides that hold liquid in. On a flat plate or a tray, soup would spill.
quests.funFact: Bowls are among the oldest dishes people have made from clay.

quests.instruction: Which of these is a tool many families use instead of a fork to pick up food?
quests.hint: It comes as a pair and is held in one hand.
quests.explanation: Chopsticks are two thin sticks used to pick up food in many countries. A ladle serves soup, and a whisk mixes batter.
quests.funFact: Some foods are eaten with fingers or scooped up with pieces of flatbread.

quests.instruction: A spoon and a fork both hold food. Why is a spoon better for soup?
quests.hint: Which part of a utensil could hold a liquid?
quests.explanation: A spoon's curved bowl scoops and carries liquid. A fork's prongs are made for picking up solid food.
quests.funFact: Spoons are older than forks. People ate with spoons long before forks became common in many places.

quests.instruction: Which bed item supports your head so your neck can rest comfortably?
quests.hint: It is small and soft and sits at the top end of the bed.
quests.explanation: A pillow lifts and cushions your head and neck. A blanket covers you, and a mattress supports your whole body.
quests.funFact: Some ancient pillows were hard stands made of wood or stone.

quests.instruction: Hana wakes up shivering on a chilly night. What could she add to her bed?
quests.hint: Work out what holds in the warmth your body makes.
quests.explanation: A blanket traps the warmth your body gives off. A pillow or a night light would not change how cold you feel.
quests.funFact: Several thin layers keep you warm because warm air stays trapped between them.

quests.instruction: Which item can wake you at the same time every morning?
quests.hint: It makes a sound at a time you choose.
quests.explanation: An alarm clock rings at the time it is set for. A night light glows in the dark, and a sheet covers the mattress.
quests.funFact: The first alarm clocks were wind-up machines that rang a small bell.

quests.instruction: Crumbs are scattered across a hard floor. Which tool gathers them into a pile?
quests.hint: It has stiff bristles on a long handle.
quests.explanation: A broom's bristles sweep dry crumbs and dust into a pile. Mops and sponges are for wet cleaning.
quests.funFact: Brooms have been made from straw, twigs, and plant fibers for hundreds of years.

quests.instruction: The crumbs are in a pile. What scoops them up off the floor?
quests.hint: It is the broom's partner, and it lies flat against the floor.
quests.explanation: A dustpan sits flat on the floor so the broom can push the pile into it. Then the pile goes in the trash.
quests.funFact: Many dustpans have a soft rubber edge, so no dust slips underneath.

quests.instruction: A sticky spot on a tiled floor is still there after sweeping. Which tool, used with water, finishes the job?
quests.hint: Sweeping cannot lift something sticky. What soaks up water?
quests.explanation: Sweeping clears dry crumbs first, and then a mop with water lifts what is stuck. Dry tools cannot remove sticky spots.
quests.funFact: Wet floors are slippery, so wait until they dry before walking across them.

quests.instruction: Which item helps wash dirt and germs off your hands when you scrub with water?
quests.hint: It makes bubbles when it mixes with water.
quests.explanation: Soap lifts dirt and germs off skin so water can rinse them away. A towel only dries, and a comb is for hair.
quests.funFact: Soap grabs onto dirt and germs so that water can wash them away.

quests.instruction: Noor steps out of the bath dripping wet. What does she need first?
quests.hint: Water on your skin can make you feel cold. What takes it away?
quests.explanation: A towel soaks up water so you can dry off and stay warm.
quests.funFact: Towels are woven with tiny loops of thread that soak up water.

quests.instruction: Why does each person in a family have their own toothbrush?
options: Each mouth needs a different size 🪥
quests.hint: Think about what could travel from one mouth to another.
quests.explanation: Sharing a toothbrush can spread germs. Everyone keeps their own and stores it where it can dry.
quests.funFact: Dentists suggest changing your toothbrush about every three months, or sooner if the bristles bend.

quests.instruction: The lights go out one evening. Which is the safer light to hold and carry?
quests.hint: Find the light that cannot start a fire.
quests.explanation: A flashlight gives light without a flame. Candles and matches can start fires, so they are only for adults to handle.
quests.funFact: A flashlight kept in a drawer that everyone knows about is ready if the power goes out.

quests.instruction: Which household item would tell you what day your cousin's party is?
quests.hint: Look for the one that lays out days in rows.
quests.explanation: A calendar lists days and months, so families can mark events on it. A scale measures weight, and a thermometer measures temperature.
quests.funFact: Lots of families write birthdays and appointments on one shared calendar.

quests.instruction: A school project needs paper cut into shapes. What is the safest way for a young child to do it?
options: Use a pair of garden shears 🌿
quests.hint: Choose a tool made for small hands, and have someone nearby.
quests.explanation: Child-safe scissors have rounded tips and are made for small hands. Knives and garden shears are far too sharp for a young child.
quests.funFact: Left-handed and right-handed scissors are shaped differently.

quests.instruction: Morning sun streams into a room while a baby naps. What can be closed to make it dimmer?
quests.hint: It hangs at the window and slides or pulls across.
quests.explanation: Curtains cover windows to block light, give privacy, and help keep rooms cooler. Rugs and fans do not block light.
quests.funFact: Thick, lined curtains can block light and also keep heat inside on cold nights.

quests.instruction: On a very hot afternoon, which item keeps the air moving so you feel cooler?
quests.hint: Its blades spin around.
quests.explanation: A fan moves air across your skin, which helps you feel cooler. It does not actually lower the room's temperature.
quests.funFact: Fans cool people, not rooms, so switching one off in an empty room saves power.

quests.instruction: Why do many homes put a rug on a hard floor?
quests.correctAnswer: It makes floors softer and warmer 🧶
options: It makes floors softer and warmer 🧶
It makes the room smell fresh 🌸
quests.hint: Think about bare feet on cold tiles.
quests.explanation: A rug adds a soft layer that feels warmer underfoot, and it can quiet the sound of footsteps.
quests.funFact: Some handmade rugs take months for a weaver to finish.

quests.instruction: Keys keep disappearing to the bottom of bags. What could give them a regular home?
quests.hint: Choose something that gives them one fixed, easy-to-see spot.
quests.explanation: A hook or a small bowl by the door gives keys a place to live, so nobody has to search. A basket of towels or a jar of crayons has a different job.
quests.funFact: A small tray by the door can hold keys, coins, and glasses so they are easy to find.

quests.instruction: A cold glass keeps leaving wet rings on the wooden table. What would protect it?
quests.hint: Put something flat between the glass and the table.
quests.explanation: A coaster soaks up drips and protects the surface from marks. A candle and a spoon rest have other jobs.
quests.funFact: Coasters are often made of cork, wood, or rubber so that they soak up drips.

quests.instruction: Little Sam cannot reach the bathroom sink. What would help him wash his hands safely?
quests.hint: Whatever he stands on must stay still when he does.
quests.explanation: A sturdy step stool lifts you to the sink without wobbling. Chairs and cushions can slip or tip, and a fall could hurt.
quests.funFact: Many step stools have a non-slip top and rubber feet.

quests.instruction: Which of these would be surprising to find in a bathroom?
quests.hint: Two of these belong to getting clean. One belongs to making a meal.
quests.explanation: Toothbrushes and towels are part of getting clean, so they live in the bathroom. A frying pan is for cooking and belongs in the kitchen.
quests.funFact: Bathrooms are damp, which is one more reason food items are kept elsewhere.

quests.instruction: A family keeps spare light bulbs, a toolbox, and a folding ladder together. Where might they be stored?
quests.hint: These are not used every day, and they should be kept out of the way.
quests.explanation: Things used only now and then are usually kept in a storage cupboard, a garage, or another out-of-the-way space. Toolboxes and ladders are for adult use.
quests.funFact: A label on the shelf where spare bulbs live means anyone can find them.

quests.instruction: Ali washes a plate, a cup, and a spoon and leaves them to drip dry. Where does the drying rack belong?
quests.hint: Think about where dishes get washed and put away.
quests.explanation: Dishes are washed and dried near the kitchen sink. Grouping objects by what they do helps you guess where they belong.
quests.funFact: Some dish racks drip straight into the sink, which saves counter space.
